binders: Universally quantify an arbitrary function profile : ℝ → ℝ and an arbitrary constant speed c ∈ ℝ.
Define q(x,t)=profile(x−c·t) for all real x,t; q is fixed by these parameters.
In the first claim, universally quantify x ∈ ℝ.
In the second and third claims, universally quantify x,t ∈ ℝ; τ is the real argument of the function differentiated in the third claim.
In the fourth claim, universally quantify x,t ∈ ℝ inside the consequent and then existentially quantify qt,qx ∈ ℝ. These witnesses may depend on profile,c,x,t; qx is nested after qt.

In the fifth claim's hypothesis, universally quantify real endpoints a,b. In its consequent, quantify a,b,t for spatial integrability, x,s,t for temporal flux integrability, and a,b,s,t for integral balance.
The variables ξ and τ denote spatial and temporal integration or differentiation arguments respectively. The variable state is a real argument of the fixed flux function F(state)=c·state.
All vector-space, norm, topology, and algebra instances in the target are fixed structures on ℝ, not additional universally quantified choices of a value space.
hypotheses: There are no regularity, integrability, sign, support, or boundedness assumptions on profile or speed for the first three conjuncts.
The fourth conjunct is conditional on profile being differentiable over ℝ at every real point.

The fifth conjunct is separately conditional on profile being interval integrable with respect to μ on every pair of finite real endpoints, where μ is the distinguished measure from Real.measureSpace.
The fourth and fifth hypotheses belong to separate implications; neither is a premise for the other.
conclusions: For every x,t ∈ ℝ, the function τ↦q(x+c·τ,τ) has derivative 0 at τ=t.
If profile is differentiable everywhere, then for every x,t ∈ ℝ there exist qt,qx ∈ ℝ such that τ↦q(x,τ) has derivative qt at t, ξ↦q(ξ,t) has derivative qx at x, and qt+c·qx=0.

If profile is interval integrable for every pair of real endpoints, then for every a,b,t ∈ ℝ the function x↦q(x,t) is interval integrable from a to b; for every x,s,t ∈ ℝ the function τ↦c·q(x,τ) is interval integrable from s to t; and for every a,b,s,t ∈ ℝ, ∫_a^b q(x,t) dμ(x) − ∫_a^b q(x,s) dμ(x) = ∫_s^t [c·q(a,τ) − c·q(b,τ)] dμ(τ), using oriented interval integrals.
mathematical_definitions: q : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ is the translated profile q(x,t)=profile(x−c·t), with x the spatial coordinate and t the time coordinate.
F : ℝ → ℝ is the linear flux F(z)=c·z.
μ denotes exactly MeasureTheory.MeasureSpace.volume selected by Real.measureSpace; this is a fixed measure, not a quantified parameter.
Interval integrability from a to b means integrability on both (a,b] and (b,a] with respect to μ.
The oriented interval integral ∫_a^b f dμ means ∫_(a,b] f dμ − ∫_(b,a] f dμ.
HasDerivAt asserts existence of an actual derivative with the stated value at the point, using the full real neighborhood rather than a one-sided or restricted-domain derivative.
The local differential equation is ∂q/∂t+c·∂q/∂x=0, encoded by existence of the two separate partial derivatives at each point.
The characteristic indexed by x is the path τ↦(x+c·τ,τ). Its index x is fixed when differentiating along the path.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For every real-valued function profile on the entire real line and every real constant c, set q(x,t)=profile(x−c·t). Five claims hold together. First, q agrees with profile at time zero. Second, q(x+c·t,t)=profile(x) for all real x,t. Third, along each path τ↦(x+c·τ,τ), the composed function has derivative zero at every real time, without any regularity assumption on profile. Fourth, if profile is differentiable everywhere, both partial derivatives of q exist at every real point and satisfy ∂q/∂t+c·∂q/∂x=0. Fifth, if profile is interval integrable with respect to the selected real measure μ on every finite interval, then every spatial slice of q and every temporal slice of its flux c·q are interval integrable, and for all real a,b,s,t the change from time s to time t in the oriented spatial integral over a to b equals the oriented time integral from s to t of the flux at a minus the flux at b.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The target is scalar-valued over ℝ. Although several dependencies allow a general real normed vector space E, that generality is not quantified in this proposition.
Space and time range over all of ℝ, including negative times. No restriction such as t≥0, a≤b, or s≤t is present.
Speed is a single constant real number and may be positive, negative, or zero; it does not depend on position, time, or state.

The first three claims hold for arbitrary profiles. The derivative along a characteristic concerns a constant composition and does not assert that profile or q has partial derivatives without the fourth hypothesis.
The fourth implication is vacuous for a profile that is not differentiable everywhere. The fifth implication is vacuous for a profile failing the stated interval-integrability hypothesis.

The differentiability hypothesis does not require a continuous derivative. The differential conclusion explicitly asserts separate partial derivatives, not continuous partial derivatives or a jointly continuous derivative field.
The integrability assumption concerns all finite intervals and does not require integrability over the entire real line, compact support, boundedness, or decay at infinity.
The temporal integrability conclusion concerns the flux c·q at fixed spatial positions. It does not separately assert temporal integrability of q; in particular, c=0 makes the flux identically zero.

Equal interval endpoints give zero oriented integrals, but the universal quantification also includes distinct endpoints, so these degenerate cases do not make the entire conservation assertion vacuous.

The target provides explicit-function identities and conditional solution properties. It does not assert uniqueness, classify all solutions, or quantify over an arbitrary solution satisfying initial data.

The conservation predicate is the displayed interval balance with slice integrability. It does not explicitly encode a distributional test-function formulation, entropy inequalities, boundary conditions, or total mass conservation on an unbounded domain.
The initial identity and characteristic identity are pointwise equalities, not merely almost-everywhere assertions. Integrability itself is a measure-theoretic property.
